title: The High Cost of Being Right
author: Jeff Matlow
source: The Best Leadership Newsletter Ever (thebestleadershipnewsletter.com), November 16, 2026
summary: Executive coach Jeff Matlow opens with a story from age 22, when he argued with the CEO of Geffen Records in a job interview and lost the job because he was so sure he was right. He uses it to argue that expertise turns into a liability for senior leaders: they hire smart people, then spend meetings proving those people wrong, until the team stops offering ideas and the leader concludes nobody else has any. Matlow traces the problem to identity, since early in a career people are rewarded for learning and later for knowing, so a challenge to an idea feels like a challenge to the self. He says this cannot be fixed by white-knuckling a new behavior, and offers a concrete experiment: when someone disagrees, ask them to explain why they think they are right, and do not offer an opinion until you can state their view well enough that they agree you understood it. The closing line reframes the stakes: being wrong does not make a leader bad, but being unwilling to find out does.
points: Knowing your stuff becomes a liability when leaders hire smart people and then spend their time explaining why those people are wrong, which teaches the team to stop sharing ideas.
The leader reads the resulting silence as proof nobody else has good ideas, which reinforces the need to have all the answers (the Pattern-Environment Loop).
Defensiveness is an identity problem, not a behavior problem: once knowing becomes who you are, a challenge to the idea feels like a challenge to you.
The practical move is to ask the dissenter to explain why they think they are right, listen, and restate their view to their satisfaction before offering your own.
quotes: I wasn’t trying to be difficult. I genuinely believed I was right. And being convinced I was right made it almost impossible for me to consider that I might be wrong.
You hire people because they’re smart. Then you spend your time proving you’re smarter.
Eventually, those smart people will stop sharing their ideas. Not because they don’t have any. But because you’ve taught them that you don’t want to hear them.
Early in your career, you’re rewarded for learning. Later, you’re rewarded for knowing. Somewhere along the way, knowing becomes part of who you are.
So when somebody challenges your idea, it doesn’t feel like they’re questioning your thinking. It feels like they’re questioning you.
You can’t fix an identity problem by white-knuckling a behavioral change.
The next time someone disagrees with you about something important, don’t explain why they’re wrong. Instead, ask them to explain why they think they’re right.
Because being wrong doesn’t make you a bad leader. Being unwilling to find out does.
